en: Pāśupatasūtra, 1:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule of yoga pertaining to Paśupati. (PS 1.1)

Having bowed my head to that Paśupati, the Lord of the Assembly, by whom the entire world beginning with Brahmā was created for the sake of [all beings'] welfare— he who is endowed with the excellence of purpose and possesses the highest excellence of knowledge—
The commentary on the fivefold meaning is composed by Kauṇḍinya in successive order.
It is said: "The Blessed One will teach the fivefold meaning.
Now, what is the first sūtra of this [work]?
To this it is replied: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the Pāśupata rule of yoga pertaining to Paśupati.
This is the first sūtra, which is recited at the beginning of the treatise.
Immediately following that, the analysis of the words (padavigraha) is performed.
"We shall explain the method of yoga conducive to that.
This is the eight-word aphorism (*sūtra*).
Among these, the two words "atha" and "ataḥ" are indeclinables (*naipātika*).
The word "of Paśupati" (paśupateḥ) is uttered in the sense of possession (*parigraha*).
"Pāśupata" is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
"The rule of yoga" (*yogavidhi*) is a compound (*sāmāsika*).
The two words "vi" and "āṅ" are nominal;
"khyāsyāmaḥ" is a verbal form.
[An objector] asks: what is the purpose for which the analysis of the words (padavigraha) is performed?
That is said for the sake of establishing the meaning.
Why is there no establishment of meaning from words?
Because in this context, words possess distinct meanings.
For it has been said thus:
"Just as a man whose limbs are uncovered does not become visible even when his head is covered,
so too a Sūtra devoid of an exposition (vigraha) does not attain manifestation."
* Thus, the analysis of words (*padavigraha*) is performed for the purpose of establishing the meaning.
// PSBh_1.1:20 * He says: The analysis of words and its purpose have been stated.
// PSBh_1.1:21 * But this must be stated: what, then, is the "treatise" (*śāstra*) and so forth? // PSBh_1.1:22

To this it is replied: "Now, therefore, [the teaching] of Paśupati"—this, first of all, is the beginning of the scripture (*śāstra*). In that context, the scripture consists of the *tantra*, the text (*grantha*), and the knowledge (*vidyā*), because both the text and its meaning serve as the means for attaining that [knowledge].
The extent [of the work] begins with the word "atha" and ends with "Śiva"; it is the teaching [of the Pāśupata system].

(PSBh 1.1:26) Its number consists of five chapters, five Brahmans, and the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*). (PSBh 1.1:27) Furthermore, from the explanation of the words "atha" and "ataḥ," and from the instruction regarding bathing, lying down, and so forth, the status of both disciple and teacher is established. (PSBh 1.1:28)

Because even those who have attained isolation (*kaivalya*) are seen to be subject to suffering, this teacher—who, being a sage (*vipra*), perceives both cause and effect and perceives both the means and the goal—answers the questions; and because he is in a state of sovereignty due to his liberation, he abides in a mind that is beyond the mind (*amanas*) because he has no desires.
Therefore, this teacher is superior to all other teachers. (PSBh 1.1:29)
Likewise, because of the mention of "brahmins," the prohibition against women, and the instruction on the conquest of the senses, it has been said:
"Deafness, blindness, loss of smell, muteness, as well as dullness, insanity, lameness, leprosy, impotence, hemorrhoids, and lameness. (PSBh 1.1:30)
A Brahmin disciple is one who is free from defects and possesses sharp faculties.
And he is distinguished from others as "this disciple.
Likewise, because gods and others possess the nature of play, the activity of the Lord is motivated by play.
The teacher’s engagement in speaking the sacred teaching is for the sake of bestowing grace.

Likewise, the student who seeks the end of suffering engages in approaching [the teacher] here because of the instruction regarding devotion, exhortation, serenity, and the desire to attain the state of Śiva.
But it is not for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, or kaivalya.

* Likewise, because he possesses desire and because he possesses a divine nature characterized by unsurpassed playful sovereignty, [he is called] Ācārya; this is the meaning. // PSBh_1.1:37 * Furthermore, Indra, Kauśika, and others are non-divine disciples because they are overwhelmed by sufferings such as being subject to injunctions (*codanā*), approaching [the teacher] (*upasadana*), and ritual purification (*saṃskāra*). // PSBh_1.1:38 * Similarly, due to the authority of the learned (*śiṣṭa-prāmāṇya*), because of his desire, and because he is unborn, the Blessed One, assuming a human form, descended in the form of a Brahmin body during his descent from the body (*kāyāvataraṇa*). // PSBh_1.1:39
Likewise, he reached Ujjayinī on foot;
why?
Because of the authority of the learned and because of seeing and hearing signs [of the city].

Having adopted a sectarian mark (liṅga) well-known among those beyond the [four] stages of life (atyāśrama), he delivered his teaching. For the sake of establishing his authority, he resided upon an altar of ashes in a pure place within a sanctuary prescribed by his own scripture, in order to associate with disciples, following the practices of ash-bathing, reclining, subsequent bathing, and wearing the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and a single garment.

Therefore, impelled by Rudra, the venerable Kuśika approached the Teacher; having perceived in the Teacher signs of complete satisfaction and excellence, while seeing the opposite signs in himself, he clasped his feet, duly announced his birth, lineage, learning, and freedom from debt, and stood before the Teacher— who was waiting for him like a physician— like a patient.

He asked, "O Blessed One, is there a definitive and absolute removal of all these sufferings— those pertaining to the self, those pertaining to living beings, and those pertaining to the divine— or is there not?

Then, having introduced the instruction by means of another's teaching for the sake of removing the desire for acquisition and authority regarding what has been taught, and for the purpose of establishing the recitation of a true disciple and practitioner, and for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the categories of causes, he made that introduction by means of another's teaching concerning the Self.
The Blessed One himself said, "Now" (atha). Here, the word "now" refers back to what was previously mentioned.
How so?
He said "atha" (then) with reference to the question previously uttered by the disciple;
thus, this word "atha" serves the purpose of providing an answer to what was asked.
Its meaning is "that which is the end of suffering."
He asked: "Was the end of suffering promised to a tested disciple, or to one who is untested? It is replied: "To the tested," because it says thus.
Here, the word *ataḥ* refers to the qualities of the disciple;
for this disciple is born in the land of Brahmāvarta, of noble family, possesses sharp faculties, and is endowed with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and other such virtues.
Furthermore, the word *ataḥ* should be understood here as having its meaning [implied] from what precedes.
Now, as to how that end of suffering is attained and by what means:
it is said [to be] through the grace of Paśupati; this is the completion of the sentence.
Here, the Lord of Paśus is Paśupati. Here, those called "paśus" are all sentient beings, with the exception of the perfected ones (siddhas) and the Lords (īśvaras).
Both those who possess the impurity of the body and organs (*kārya-karaṇa-añjana*) and those who are stainless (*nirañjana*) are paśus.
He asks: "What is their state of being cattle (paśutva)?
It is replied: Bondage is lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya).
Lack of sovereignty, characterized by the suppression of the power of the cause and consisting of a lack of self-mastery, is bondage; it is not a physical cord.

It is metaphorically designated as the "quality of bondage. If one asks what its characteristics are, it is said: they are called *paśus* (bound souls) because of their seeing (*paśyanā*) and their being bound (*pāśanā*).
In this context, "fetter" (*pāśa*) refers to the *kalās* known as the effect and the instrument.
We shall explain those *kalās* further below.

Bound, fettered, and completely constrained by them, [the souls] remain subject to external objects such as sound and so forth; from this it is understood that lack of autonomy and lack of sovereignty constitute bondage.

If it is argued that the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) ceases for one who is devoid of the body and its instruments, it is said in response: according to the scripture, even for those [instruments] that have been withdrawn, there is a repeated grasping of their connection.
Furthermore:
And they are called "beasts" (paśu) because of their seeing;
for although they possess omnipresence and inherence in consciousness, they see and perceive only the body itself and nothing external.
Furthermore, being devoid of organs of action, they neither acquire nor abandon organs of action.
And because they depend upon the revelation of dharma and adharma, as well as place, time, injunctions, and so forth;
therefore it is well said that they are "bound" (paśavaḥ) due to seeing (paśyanāt) and being bound (pāśanāt).
For it has been stated: "Those who are liberated through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and those who are masters of Sāṃkhya and Yoga..."
All beings, from Brahmā down to the animals, are remembered as *paśus* (bound souls).
Why is he the *pati* (Lord)?
Because he attains (*āpti*) and protects (*pāti*) those *paśus*, he is therefore the *pati*.
By what does one obtain them, and by what does one protect them? It is by the power of the pervasive Lord (vibhu-śakti),
because even there, they do not transcend his infinite power.
And because he is a Brahmin, his power of knowledge is infinite and immeasurable;

by means of that immeasurable [power], he attains as many perceptible sacrificial animals as are immeasurable, and thus he is the "Lord" (pati). Likewise, because he protects them, he possesses the power of mastery (prabhu-śakti).
Why?

Because from that [unseen force], their engagement and withdrawal, as well as their stability and the attainment of desired or undesired locations, bodies, sense organs, objects, and so forth, come about;
the meaning is that these occur for those who are perceived by it and impelled by it. Thus. (PSBh 1.1:42)
The phrase "of Paśupati" is an enumeration of the cause, the effect, and the grace;
the meaning is that from that grace, that end of suffering is attained,
and not merely through knowledge, dispassion, dharma, or the renunciation of sovereignty.
He asked: "In what state, at what time, or of what kind must one be for that Blessed One to become pleased?
It is said in reply: "When he has attained that.
He asked: "What is that?"
It is said that it is called *Pāśupata* because it was spoken by Paśupati, accepted [by him], and commenced with reference to Paśupati;
just as [the systems] are called Vaiṣṇava or Mānasa.
What is it?
It is said: "Yoga.
Here, yoga is the conjunction of the self (ātman) and the Lord (īśvara).
Furthermore, because it is occasioned by the person's study and other such means, it arises from the action of one of the two parties, like [the contact between] a post and a hawk.
Based on statements such as those concerning the impelling [of the soul] and the study [of the Vedas], conjunction is produced by the actions of both [the soul and the body], like that of two rams;
for even though [the soul] possesses omnipresence, disjunction is not caused by an absence of qualification [to act],
and it is precisely the disjoined [soul] that is taught to enter into conjunction.

Just as there is application of action for one who is either attached to or detached from sense objects, here, however, in the yoga characterized by meditative concentration (samādhi), there is "restraint" (saṃniyama).
He asks: Is that yoga attained merely through full comprehension?
It is said:
because it says, "We shall explain the method for attaining that.
Here, "the method of yoga" (*yogavidhi*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "the method belonging to yoga."
In this context, the designation "rite" (*vidhi*) applies to subtle, gross, external, internal, and both similar and dissimilar actions, just like the injunctions for sacrifice (*yajñavidhi*);
it does not apply [to them] as one would to an army or a forest.
Why?
Because a collection of momentary actions is impossible,
if this is so, why is it called a "prescription" (vidhi)? It is called a prescription because it prescribes.
And because of the relationship between the means and the end:
"method" (vidhi) refers to the action.
Thus, the object of suffering, the end of suffering, the effect, the cause, and yoga as the method—these five categories have been briefly enumerated.
These are to be explained;
the explanation of these consists of the detailed analysis, the specific distinctions, the summary, and the conclusion.
Therefore, that which is to be explained is one thing, and the explanation is another.
For it says, "we shall explain" (vyākhyāsyāmaḥ).
Here, the prefix *vi-* occurs in the senses of expansion (*vistara*), analysis (*vibhāga*), and distinction (*viśeṣa*).
Among these, "expansion" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are stated to be perception (*māna*), authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*), and so forth.
Among these, perception is twofold: sensory perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*) and self-perception (*ātmapratyakṣa*).
Sensory perception is established through the objects of the senses—sound, touch, form, taste, smell, jars, food, explanations, heat, urine, feces, flesh, salt, and breath-control.
The direct perception of the self is established by such scriptural statements as "the end of suffering through the totality of penances offered to it.
For example, rice measured by a *prastha* [measure] is called a *prastha*.

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises when the causal complex that manifests the connection between the sense organs and their objects is assisted by merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), illumination, place, time, injunctions, and so forth.

Self-perception (*ātmapratyakṣa*), however, consists in the causal complex of the connection between the mind (*citta*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the self. Inference (*anumāna*) is also preceded by perception; it likewise consists in the causal complex of the connection between the mind, the self, and the internal organ, and has as its causes merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), light, place, time, injunctions, and so forth, as well as memory. Through these—such as the times of origination, maintenance, and dissolution—the agency of the Cause in subsequent creation is inferred.
Therefore, it is not contrary to the Sūtra.
Furthermore, that [inference] is of two kinds: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the generally perceived (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Among these, the perceived is also of two kinds: the "prior" (*pūrvavat*) and the "residual" (*śeṣavat*).
In this regard, the inference "this six-finger-ring is that very same one previously seen" is *pūrvavat* (based on what was previously perceived).
The inference "it is a cow" from seeing only its horns and so forth is *śeṣavat* (based on the remainder).

*Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is also found here: having observed that reaching another location is preceded by motion, the existence of motion in the sun and other celestial bodies is established.

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause for the comprehension of an object even across the three periods of time. Tradition (*āgama*) refers to a scripture that has come down through a lineage of teachers up to Maheśvara.
Tradition is declared and remembered as the cause for non-worldly and other such conventional practices.
Rudra declared that perfection comes from speech;
within these very [means of knowledge] is included the explanation of comparison, presumption, postulation, non-existence, tradition, intuition, and so forth.
Thus, there are these three means of valid cognition.
The Blessed One is the one who causes valid cognition;
the questioner is the cognizer;
and the objects of cognition are the five categories, beginning with cause and effect.
Valid cognition (pramiti) is consciousness (saṃvit).
Consciousness means thorough reflection, awakening, and the manifestation of knowledge; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, from the understanding of the brief statement and the detailed exposition, there arises an extensive [treatise].

"Division" (vibhāga) means the non-confusion of words, word-meanings, aphorisms, chapters, sections, and so forth. "Distinction" (viśeṣa) means the differentiation between the probandum and the probans.
The prefix "ā-" is used in the sense of the limit of an exposition.

We shall explain [the text] step by step—verse by verse, sutra by sutra, section by section, chapter by chapter—from the beginning until awakening and until completion; and we shall do so specifically for one who remains within the bounds of the discipline.
The root *khyā* means "to declare.
We shall provide an exposition using both well-known and less well-known designations, and by means of methods distinct from those prescribed in the Vedas and other such sources.
The word *syāt* refers to a future time.

As long as this teacher prepares—by means of ash consecrated with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras—a Brāhmaṇa who has previously arrived from householders and others, and who has been examined by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), for the purpose of a vow, fast, or similar rite, at the southern image of Mahādeva; so long [he remains].
Having performed the withdrawal of the signs of birth and having caused the recitation of the mantra, the time for the "approaching" (eṣya) is established;
this occurs within the vow of "ma.
For one who is correctly established in the group beginning with rising and so forth, the Blessed One himself is the speaker, in due order, of both the subject to be explained and the explanation.

Since the comprehension of subtle objects of discipline is preceded by gross means, the injunction is explained first for the purpose of prohibiting the restrictive rules of the previous stages of life (*āśrama*) and for the purpose of establishing the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) of the *atyāśrama*.
Thus, this presentation of the meaning of the words [in the first sūtra] is concluded.
Here, one who has grasped the portion [of the meaning] says: "The injunction is explained first according to the rule."
This must now be considered:

what is its beginning, what is its middle, what is its end, and how many constituent parts does the ritual have? To this it is replied: the ritual has ash as its beginning, censure as its middle, and delusion as its end.
And that [sacrifice] has three constituent parts: giving (*dāna*), sacrificing (*yajana*), and austerity (*tapas*).
How is this understood? Because the following is commenced:
"One should bathe with ashes at the three sessions of the day. (PS 1.2)

In this context, ash is the substance to be used on the left, which is produced from the conjunction of fire and fuel. That [ash] should be prepared by others, be of earthly origin, consumed, and radiant.
The collection of ash should be performed like the gathering of alms from villages and other such places.

Because of the requirements of bathing, lying down, post-bathing rites, and association with kinsmen; because of the absence of possessions; and because of non-violence, only that which is excellent, pure, and abundant should be accepted for the purpose of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
(PSBh 1.2:4) If these are not obtained, even a small amount may be accepted.
(PSBh 1.2:5) In this context, the vessel is also well known to be made of gourd, leather, cloth, or similar materials. (PSBh 1.2:6)

[The opponent] asks: "What is to be done with that ash? This is replied to: The instrumental case in the word "bhasmanā" (with ash) indicates the instrument for the purpose of expressing the agent's action, just as an axe is used for the act of carving, or as the mind is used for the act of covering. [The opponent] asks: "Then at what time should that action be performed?"
"Triṣavaṇam" [is] a dvigu compound. "Trīṇi" is a numeral.
*Savana* is a designation for time.
The three *saṃdhyās* are the morning twilight (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*), the midday twilight (*madhyāhnasaṃdhyā*), and the evening twilight (*aparasaṃdhyā*).
*Triṣavaṇa*, *trisaṃdhya*, and *trikāla* have the same meaning [i.e., the three times].
He asks: "What is to be done by him at the three sessions?
This is said: "He should bathe.
Here, bathing for the purpose of purification consists of removing from the body adventitious moisture, skin-grease, dirt, odor, and so forth, by means of ashes.
"Bathing, moreover, is the application of the substance of ashes to the body.

(PSBh 1.2:19) "But from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), since bathing and so forth are spoken of as having the nature of dharma through their connection with the fruits of merit, this is indeed the purification of the self (*ātmaśauca*). (PSBh 1.2:20) "However, by means of the designation of the body and its instruments (*kāryakaraṇa*), the purification of the self is explained through such expressions as 'bathing alone' and 'the removal of impurities and sins. (PSBh 1.2:21)
The word *ita* is used in the senses of command (*ājñā*) and injunction (*niyoga*).
Because it is an injunction (*niyoga*), it is "gone forth" (*nigata*); because it is restricted (*niyata*), the meaning is "Veda" (*nigama*). Why? [Because it is the source of all injunctions.]
Because it is established by its own system (*pratitantra*), because it is non-violent (*ahiṃsaka*), and because it is a cause for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
(PSBh 1.2:25) One should bathe with ashes and not with water; the meaning is that [water] is the opposite [of the required qualities].
(PSBh 1.2:26) Is it the case that bathing itself must be performed with ashes in this manner? (PSBh 1.2:27)
It is said:
Because it says:
"He should sleep on ashes. (PS 1.3)
* Here, "ashes" refers to that very same thing.
(PSBh 1.3:1) * Its etymological explanation has been stated previously. (PSBh 1.3:2) * "In the ashes" indicates proximity by way of contact (*aupaśleṣika-saṃnidhāna*). (PSBh 1.3:3)

The word *śaya* is a designation for tranquility and rest. The word *ita* is used in the sense of a command or an injunction. The meaning is that one must sleep only on ashes at night, and not elsewhere.

For it has been said: "Just as deer, terrified by the fear of death, find no sleep due to their agitated dwelling, so too the high-souled ascetic devoted to meditation, fearing cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), finds no sleep.
Furthermore, it is because of his pursuit of excellence.
And this Brahmin is one who seeks excellence.
For it has been said: "For those who seek excellence, sleep does not remain long in their eyes, just as for noble horses that sleep only half a watch at midnight."

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: on a ground that has been well-sprinkled, having performed the ritual enclosure during the day and having spread ashes, one who is intent upon study, teaching, and meditation, and exhausted by devotion to the contemplation of the sacred teachings, should sleep at night with his arm used as a pillow upon the ashes consecrated with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras.
If it is asked, "For what purpose?
it is said: for the sake of austerity, for the sake of purification on a portion of ground, or for the sake of rest.
The meaning is that one should sleep for one watch or two watches on ground that is level, uneven, low, or high.
Bathing after [the meal]. // PS_1.4 //

* Like the bathing performed with mantras and so forth. // PSBh_1.4:1 * Here, the word "anu" (after) occurs in the sense of a subsequent action. // PSBh_1.4:2 * It is like drinking after [eating] or following after [someone]. // PSBh_1.4:3

*The bath, however, consists precisely in the application of the substance of ashes.* (PSBh 1.4:4) *Having observed the impurity caused by such factors as eating, being left-over from a meal, sneezing, spitting, or the voiding of urine and feces during the intervals between the three daily baths, one must perform a subsequent bath (anusnāna).* (PSBh 1.4:5) *If it is asked for what purpose: it is for the sake of purification and for the sake of manifesting the [divine] signs.* (PSBh 1.4:6)
The meaning is that it should be smeared.
He asks: Is ash alone the cause for manifesting the *liṅga*?
Or, when devotion has increased, why is there no means [for manifestation] for one who is not prohibited?
That is said:
* Here, "nirmālya" refers to that which is well-known in the world and other contexts as ashes (bhasma).
// PSBh_1.5:1 * "Nir" is a designation for that which is released (nirmukta).
// PSBh_1.5:2 * "Mālya" is a synonym for a cluster of flowers (puṣpasamūha). // PSBh_1.5:3

That [lotus, blue lotus, and so forth], which has been fashioned by another, is placed upon and then brought down from the form of the causal deity; it is without personal ownership. The meaning is that this should be worn for the sake of increasing devotion and for the sake of manifesting the [divine] sign (*liṅga*). He asks: "Where is it established that his sign is manifested by means of ashes and flower-garlands?"
This is stated here:
because it says—*liṅgadhārī* (the bearer of the marks). 1.6.

In this regard, just as there are marks that distinguish the various stages of life (*āśrama*) for other members of the social classes (*varṇa*), [so it is here]. Among them, first, the marks of the householder (*gṛhastha*) are: three garments, a bamboo staff, a water-pot with water, the shaving of the upper lip, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth. Likewise, the marks of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) are: a staff, a water-pot, a girdle made of muñja grass, the sacred thread, a black antelope skin, and so forth.
Likewise, for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the marks (*liṅga*) consist of wearing the *karīra* fruit, bark garments, matted hair, and so forth.

Similarly, for the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), the marks consist of the triple staff, the shaven head, the water-pot, saffron-colored robes, the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*), the ground-strainer (*sthalapavitra*), and so forth.

In the same way, here too, this mark—which is the subject-matter of the *Pāśupata-yoga* and which serves to distinguish the various stages of life (*āśrama*)—is established by means of ash-baths, lying down [in ashes], post-bathing rites, the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), wearing a single garment, and other such practices.

The Pāśupata [knowledge] is that which is merged within one's own body and generates worldly and other forms of knowledge. It is called a *liṅga* because of its merging (*līyanāt*) and its indicating (*liṅganāt*).
One who bears that [knowledge] becomes a bearer of the *liṅga* (*liṅgadhārī*).
The meaning is "like a staff-bearer.
[The opponent] asks: Now, where should these matters—the bathing, the reclining, the subsequent bathing, and so forth—be performed?
Or from where should the acquisition of the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) be carried out?
* Where should that [staff] be carried by one who has taken up the insignia? * Or where should one who has assumed the marks dwell?
* To this it is replied: in a monastery (āyatana).
For it says:
"One who dwells in the sense-bases" (PS 1.7).
Now, the term *āyatana* refers to that which is well-known in the world and elsewhere as being like ashes or discarded flower-garlands.
(PSBh 1.7:1) The prefix *āṅ* is used here in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*).

(PSBh 1.7:2) For these householders and others, who are characterized by effort, restraint, purity, and virtuous conduct, abide according to their respective limits and perform sacrifices through rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). (PSBh 1.7:3)
"And because of sacrifice, [he is] a dweller in a sacred site (āyatanavāsī).
(PS 1.7) He should dwell in a sacred site prepared by others; thus, he accepts a sacred site as his dwelling.

Dwelling anywhere—in a region of the earth, in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or outside [a village]—while proceeding clockwise according to the conduct of the learned, he becomes a dweller in a sacred site. (PSBh 1.7:5–6)
The meaning is that one should dwell as if dwelling on a sandbank.
And the attainment of the fruit of merit occurs for him quickly.
For it has been said: "Whether in a village or in a forest, [it is] indeed a sacred place of the Wielder of the Trident."
"This is the abode of those satisfied with the Dharma; for it is the supreme field of accomplishment.
[Objection: What rites should be performed by one dwelling in that sanctuary?
Are they bathing and so forth, or anointing with ointments and so forth?
Or rather, have other specific rites to be performed by him been observed?
We shall explain how other specific rites are to be performed and what their purpose is:
One should attend upon [the deity] with offerings consisting of laughter, song, dance, the sound "duṃ-duṃ," prostrations, recitation, and oblations. (PS 1.8)
Now, having bathed at the three times for bathing with ashes consecrated by the *sadyojāta* mantra and so forth while reciting [the mantra], one should approach the sanctuary while still reciting it.
(PSBh 1.8:1) And having approached, that which one recites first is the mantra to be recited for the purpose of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*): *oṃ oṃ oṃ*.
(PSBh 1.8:2) But that which one recites afterwards after performing laughter and so forth is the mantra to be recited for the purpose of restraint (*niyama*). (PSBh 1.8:3)

*In this context, that which is called "laughter" (*hasita*) is when a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*) is produced by the expansion of the throat and lips; that is laughter. (PSBh 1.8:4) *Singing* (*gīta*) also refers to that wherein the names of the Blessed Lord Maheśvara—derived from qualities, substances, and actions—are contemplated in the assembly, without attachment to the conventions of the science of music (*gāndharvaśāstra*). (PSBh 1.8:5) *That which is sung*, whether in Sanskrit, Prakrit, composed by others, or composed by oneself, is what constitutes song (*geya*). (PSBh 1.8:6)

*Dance (*nṛtta*) also consists of the raising, lowering, contracting, extending, moving, and shifting of the hands, feet, and other limbs, without being bound by the conventions of the treatises on dramatic performance (*nāṭyaśāstra*). (PSBh 1.8:7) At the time of the recitation (*nigama*), dance should be performed accompanied by song for the sake of establishing the proper rhythm (*niyama*).
(PSBh 1.8:8) That which is produced by the contact of the tip of the tongue with the palate is called the *ḍuṃḍuṃkāra*; it is meritorious and resembles the bellowing of a bull. (PSBh 1.8:9)

*The utterance "ḍuṃḍuṃ" is "ḍuṃḍuṃkāraḥ."* (PSBh 1.8:10) *The word "kāra" is intended to determine that [the sound] "ḍuṃḍuṃ" is a constituent part of the offering.* (PSBh 1.8:11) *"[The word] 'namaḥ'..."* (PSBh 1.8:12)
Nor should it be performed with the lips, nor in a whisper.
But the salutation is a mental act of homage.
The word "kāra" is for the purpose of excluding vocal and whispered [utterances], and for the purpose of determining that the mental offering is the essential constituent; such is the meaning.
*Japya* refers to the mental movement and reflection upon the state [of the deity] within the sequence of syllables beginning with Sadyojāta.
That is what is to be muttered (*japya*).
The prefix *upa-* functions as a qualifier in the sense of bringing an action to completion and in the sense of totality.

*Upahāra* means bringing near; its meaning is a vow (*vrata*) or a restrictive observance (*niyama*). (PSBh 1.8:19) It is called *upahāra* because it is offered or presented by the practitioner, who acts solely as the agent of the injunction. (PSBh 1.8:20) One should stand in attendance (*upatiṣṭhet*). (PSBh 1.8:21)
*Atropety* means "in the case of acceptance.

*Abhyupagatena* means by one who has accepted [the practice] and stands in accordance with the rule; the sense is "by one who is bowed down and humble. *Tiṣṭhet* refers specifically to the state of remaining in one-pointedness, which is the absence of withdrawal [from the object].
Having withdrawn the activity of all the senses, one should offer service through physical, vocal, and mental actions, remaining like a servant by means of such offerings.

(PSBh 1.8:25) And we shall explain later that circumambulation is performed keeping the right side toward the object. (PSBh 1.8:26) It is asked: Whose remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) should be worn? (PSBh 1.8:27)
In whose abode should one dwell?
And where should one offer service?
This is now explained.
Of Mahādeva, the Right-Faced One (Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

* Here, "great" (*mahān*) refers to being superior (*abhyadhikatve*). (PSBh 1.9:1) He is superior, excellent, and distinct from all *kṣetrajñas*; thus he is "superior. (PSBh 1.9:2) He is a seer (*ṛṣi*), a sage (*vipra*), and a sovereign lord (*adhipati*). (PSBh 1.9:3)
We shall now explain the state of Sadāśiva and its superiority.
Here, "Deva" [is derived from] the root *div*, meaning "to play.
This is because he possesses the nature of play (*krīḍā*).

*Like the heat of fire.* (PSBh 1.9:7) The Lord, being indeed possessed of play (*krīḍāvān*), produces, favors, and conceals the threefold effect known as knowledge (*vidyā*), limited power (*kalā*), and the individual soul (*paśu*). For it has been said: "The Lord, who acts according to His own will, is not to be impelled by others, though He may impel those who are to be impelled. (PSBh 1.9:8)
The Blessed One plays with the worlds as a child plays with toys. The word "of the God" (*devasya*) is in the genitive case. The relationship [indicated] is that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*).
It is for the sake of appropriation alone that [the Lord] exercises authority.
In this context, "south" occurs as a specific division of the directions.
The sun divides the directions.
And they divide the directions according to his form (*mūrti*).
What is called "form" is that appearance which is perceived nearby on the right side of the Lord, standing and facing north—
characterized by the bull-bannered one, the trident-wielder, Nandin, Mahākāla, the upward-pointing linga, and so forth— or that which worldly people recognize.

"It is the abode of Mahādeva"—thus it should be attended there. (PSBh 1.9:16) By the mention of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [form], the [other] forms—eastern, northern, and western—are excluded. (PSBh 1.9:17) And because of the restriction to a specific form, there is a lapse of the rule in the absence of that form. (PSBh 1.9:18)
The meaning is that [this is so] because of the non-utility of alms and because it has been stated that [alms] are for those who have cast off [all worldly ties].

(PSBh 1.9:19) "Prescription" (vidhi) means that when certain matters have been taught, there is a prohibition of bathing in water and the like, because of the teaching of bathing with ashes. (PSBh 1.9:20) Because of the teaching of sleeping on ashes, there is a prohibition of sleeping in [sensual] objects and the like. (PSBh 1.9:21)
* By the teaching regarding dwelling in the sacred precinct (*āyatana*), there is a prohibition against dwelling elsewhere for that purpose.
// PSBh_1.9:22 * By the teaching regarding laughter and so forth, there is a prohibition against other offerings.
// PSBh_1.9:23 * By the teaching regarding the floral remains (*nirmālya*), there is a prohibition against fresh garlands. // PSBh_1.9:24
* By the instruction regarding the liṅga made of ashes and the discarded flower-garland, there is a prohibition of other [types of] liṅgas.
// PSBh_1.9:25 * By the mention of Mahādeva, there is a prohibition of devotion to other deities.
// PSBh_1.9:26 * By the mention of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, there is a prohibition of the eastern and western forms. // PSBh_1.9:27
Thus, when "Dakṣiṇāmūrti" is uttered, the previously established rules of this Brāhmaṇa are set aside by these [new] rules,
like a peg and its counter-peg, or like old water and new water.
Herein ends this section on the sacred ash (bhasma).
He said: "For doubt arises precisely from the mention of *niyama*.
Where there are *yamas*, there are *niyamas*, because these two constitute a pair."
Therefore, there is no doubt.
What kinds of restraints (*yama*) are considered in this treatise?
It is said that the well-known restraints are non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth.
In this regard, however, for others:
non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness, refraining from worldly dealings, and non-stealing— these five are indeed proclaimed as the restraints (yamas).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and vigilance— these five are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas).
Likewise, these do not exist for us.
Why?
Because the cessation of restrictive rules is observed.
For in this system, restrictive rules that were suspended for a period of time are now terminated.
How is it that for those who are being restrained, there is no cessation until the fall of the body?
Why?
Because of defects such as violence and the like.
Therefore, all those ten [virtues] beginning with non-violence are to be understood as the *yamas*. [Objection:
If this is so, then for one who has ceased from the village life (*nigama*) but has fallen away from the observance (*niyama*), there would be the consequence of a downfall (*patana*).
[Reply: It is said: because his purpose has been accomplished, there is no consequence of a downfall.
Furthermore, because the *yamas* are predominant:
"For it is said: 'One who possesses the *niyamas* but is not attached to the *yamas* falls; however, one who possesses the *yamas* does not perish even if he is lazy regarding the *niyamas*.
Thus, having reflected upon both *yama* and *niyama* with the intellect, one should direct the intellect toward those practices in which *yama* predominates. (PSBh_1.9:50–52)
Therefore, there is no consequence of falling [from one's status].
Hence, the restraints (*yama*), such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest, are well-established.
[The opponent] asks: Are they accepted simply because they are well-established, or can the existence of these restraints be stated on the basis of the scriptures taught by the Omniscient One?
It is said: "If [the word] is well-established elsewhere, where [is it so]?
Regarding this, it is considered:
"Why?"
* Because of the instruction given [in the following].

// PSBh 1.9:59 * Since it is stated in the Sūtra regarding the word "performed" (*kṛta*) [as follows]: // PSBh 1.9:60 * The meaning is that all violence (*hiṃsā*), which has not been specifically prohibited, is to be understood as prohibited in this treatise (*tantra*). // PSBh 1.9:61
And that violence (*hiṃsā*) is of three kinds:
the production of suffering, the breaking of eggs, and the severing of life-breaths.

Among these, "the production of suffering" refers to malice toward any of the four classes of living beings through actions of mind, speech, or body—though it has many subdivisions such as shouting, threatening, beating, and reviling.
In this way, there is non-violence toward these living beings.

Regarding what is called "avoiding the breaking of eggs," one should not perform, nor cause others to perform, actions such as lighting fires, taking them up, handing them over, placing them down, or fanning them, for the purpose of avoiding burning, affliction, or obstruction by smoke. Likewise, regarding what is called "releasing [beings from] life," items such as clothing, baskets, ash-trays, alms-bowls, and so forth, must be inspected repeatedly.
Why?
Because living beings that move subtly perish very quickly.
Therefore, one should [purify] repeatedly with subtle limb-purifiers such as eyelashes, yak-tail whisks, palm-leaf fans, or the hem of a garment, or with water from a strainer.
It should not take place on green grass or on ground that has been moistened. (PSBh 1.9:71) A monk should travel during the eight months of spring, summer, and autumn.
(PSBh 1.9:72) For the sake of compassion toward all living beings, he should dwell in one place during the rainy season. (PSBh 1.9:73)
But the Brahmin who has been initiated into yoga and should violate the rule regarding the rainy season is liberated from that sin by performing the Prājāpatya penance.
Wherever physical danger is perceived in some calamity, [one should act accordingly].
One may pass through [these times] even during foul weather, the collapse of the kingdom, or the rainy season.
One should not travel on a path without the sun, nor tread upon ground that has not been inspected.
And one should always make use of water that is completely purified.
Whatever sin a fisherman may commit in a year, one who collects impure water incurs that very same [sin] in a single day.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth and practice that which is purified by the mind.
Even those who have attained the state of Brahman turn away from violence;
therefore, the knower of yoga should not use water that is unpurified.
Now, if the strainers are lost, one should take [water] three times from a river or a spring, and once from virtuous householders; likewise,
one may take [water from] plant stalks that are gathered and from sprouting tubers.
One should avoid all these [types of] seeds that have ripened. When one does not commit any cruel injury toward any living beings through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
He who does not harm living beings, whether stationary or moving,
treating them all as he does himself, is fit for immortality.
Not by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by the Agnihotra fire-rituals, nor by vows of celibacy, nor by truthful speech [is this attained].

The fruit that is obtained by one who practices non-violence cannot be attained through the study of the Vedas and sciences, nor by religious observances. (PSBh 1.9:84) Even if one were to give away Mount Meru made of gold, the entire earth, or an ocean filled with jewels, it would not be equal to non-violence. (PSBh 1.9:85)
Thus, non-violence is established in this system;
likewise, celibacy is also established in this system.
Why? Because...

Because of the prohibition against women and because of the instruction for the conquest of the senses, it has been stated that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the non-emission of the thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*).
However, [this applies] specifically to the tongue and the generative organ.
Here, one asks: what is the purpose of mentioning "specifically"?
Having stated that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists in the non-abandonment of the thirteen instruments, for what purpose is a specific mention made of the tongue and the genitals?
It is said: because they are primary;
because the engagement of the others is rooted in them.
For the activity of others is rooted in that.
How so?
One who is attached to the object of the tongue-faculty or the object of the organ of generation proceeds by means of thirteen [faculties].
Therefore, this has been stated specifically regarding the tongue and the genitals:
"For the downfall of all embodied beings is caused by the tongue and the genitals;
therefore, a person should regard the tongue and the genitals as enemies. (PS 1.9–10)
Alternatively, since all mental functions are preceded by the mind, by restraining that [mind], the restraint of all functions is accomplished.
For it has been said: "The mind is indeed the root in the operation of all the sense-faculties;
and that [mind] of mine is well-established amidst both auspicious and inauspicious states."
It has been said again:
"Suffering arises from the senses when they are directed outward; happiness arises from the senses when they are restrained.
Therefore, one should by oneself sever the self from the forms of the senses. (PS 1.9)
For all that constitutes both heaven and hell consists of the sense-faculties;
when restrained or unleashed, they lead to heaven and to hell respectively.
From this [arises] birth, from this arises suffering, and likewise from this arises the fear of death.
Therefore, we shall indeed conquer these [senses],
for through attachment to the senses one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by thoroughly restraining them, one attains perfection.
This mind that delights in women is a rope for binding;
the wise, having cut it, go forth, but the doer of evil does not abandon it.
For the sake of women there is departure from the village; for the sake of women there is buying and selling.
Women are the root of misfortunes; a wise man should not embrace them.
This woman whom people consider to be a woman is clearly a deceptive illusion in a beautiful form—like poison, fire, a sword, or an arrow, acting as a mere source of terror.
In this body, which is filled with impurities, teeming with worms and insects, naturally foul-smelling, unclean, impermanent,
a mere carcass, and a vessel for urine and excrement— the foolish take delight, but the wise do not.
One becomes intoxicated upon seeing a woman, yet one does not become intoxicated by drinking liquor.

Therefore, one should avoid from afar a woman intoxicated by her own beauty. The world has been bitten by the serpent of the female organ, which moves between the thighs, has its mouth turned downward, lacks fangs, and cannot be cured even by all the treatises.
By one who is hairy, misshapen, foul-smelling, with poor skin, and possessing feet like those of a doe, the entire world has been blinded.
A woman is like glowing coals; a man is like a jar of clarified butter.
Those who were attached have dissolved; those who remained have gone to heaven.
Just as a fire fed with fuel shines forth as a great light, so too, through the restraint of the senses, the light of one's own self shines forth.
Fortitude is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy. Those Brahmins who abide by means of celibacy are established in heaven.
They drink milk, they drink honey, they drink Soma together with the nectar of immortality.

"Those Brahmins who practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*) become immortal even before death. Thus, celibacy is established as a proven principle in this system (*tantra*). Likewise, truthfulness is established as a proven principle in this system.
And that [truth] is of two kinds:
namely, speech whose object is perceived and whose object is real, and verbal truth (*vāksatya*).
Among these, speech whose object is perceived and whose object is real is established as truth in the *Tantra*.
Why?
Because of the explanation and the instruction, and because of the instruction of the learned.
Likewise, the truth of speech is also established in the Tantra.
Why?
Because of the instruction regarding the purity of speech.
In this context, even that which is spoken as untruth according to one's own scriptures becomes truth.
Why?
Because it produces purity and growth.
For it has been said: "One goes to heaven by means of untruth spoken for the sake of compassion toward all living beings."
Even a truth, when spoken for the purpose of destroying the virtuous, does not lead [to a good result].
Furthermore, he said to you:
"O King, silence [is preferable] for the sake of cows and Brahmins; it does not harm [to speak the truth] regarding women, nor at the time of marriage."
In cases where life is at stake, when all one's wealth is being seized, or regarding the five [specific] falsehoods, they say these are not sins.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth;
nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.

For just as for those very beings, even an untruth becomes truth when it is for their benefit, so too here, even an untruth spoken by us becomes truth when it is stated in accordance with our own Teacher’s scripture.
Why?
Because it is prescribed by the injunction.
This [point] is also established therein.
Likewise, non-transactional usage is established in the treatise.
Why? Because...

*Because of instruction by the unmanifested, the deceased, the insane, and the deluded.* (PS 1.9) In this world, the unmanifested, the deceased, the insane, and the deluded do not engage in social intercourse; therefore, it is established in the Tantra that there is no social intercourse with them here.
(PSBh 1.9:140) Furthermore, social intercourse is of two kinds. (PSBh 1.9:141)

Namely: transactions involving buying and selling, and transactions involving the royal court. Therefore, for one engaged in either of these, self-affliction and affliction of others become unavoidable. In that regard, if one afflicts oneself, by that means one becomes miserable in this very world.
Even if one should cause harm to another, in that case as well, unrighteousness (*adharma*) which has suffering and so forth as its fruit is accumulated for him.
By means of that, he experiences intense suffering in the next world.
Therefore, in either case, conventional worldly practice (*saṃvyavahāra*) is to be avoided.
For it is also said:
"He who commits a sin, he who praises the sin, his accomplice, and the one who enjoys the fruit—all of them are equal in their karma. (PSBh 1.9:148)
For it has been said: "In selling, however, there is great fault, since one falls [from dharma] because of selling;
this very same fault exists in buying. Therefore, one should avoid it.
"One commits a sin in secret, thinking, 'No one knows of me.'"
One is released from the talk of people, yet one is not thereby released from sin.
It is said again:
"The sun, the moon, the wind, the fire, the sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, and Yama—"

Day and night, and both twilights— Dharma indeed knows the conduct of a man. One who is not habituated to worldly undertakings nor habituated to hypocrisy, who performs the duties taught in the scriptures without dejection, and who is intent upon the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas)— such a sage becomes undecaying and immortal through these.
Likewise, non-stealing is established in the Tantra.
Why?
Because of the instruction not to dwell [in one place] and because of the prohibition against food that has not been offered.
In this context, although a single garment may still be present, because it is taught that one should not dwell in it when it has become soiled, the relinquishing of what has been accepted is taught.
Furthermore:
since the use of food, drink, and other such things is observed even after they have been relinquished.
Therefore, non-stealing is established here as a rule in this system.
Furthermore, stealing is of six kinds:

taking what is not given, seizing what has not been surrendered, seizing what is not consented to, accepting what one is not authorized to receive, receiving without invitation, and using what has not been offered.

Taking what has not been given is the act of seizing that which is not given. (PSBh 1.9:162) Seizing what has not been bestowed means the misappropriation of the wealth of children, the insane, the intoxicated, the aged, and the weak. (PSBh 1.9:163) Seizing what is not intended means the taking away of things undesired by insects, bees, birds, moths, and so forth. (PSBh 1.9:164)

*Receiving what one has no authority to receive* means, in this treatise, the taking of things not permitted—such as cattle, land, gold, bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth. *Non-reproach* means the employment of means such as trickery, deceit, hypocrisy, causing amazement, or offering congratulations to conceal [one's faults] from others.

*Using without having announced* means that when one consumes any of the various kinds of food—whether it be solid food (*bhakṣya*), soft food (*bhojya*), food to be licked (*lehya*), food to be drunk (*peya*), or food to be sucked (*coṣya*)—without having first announced it to the teacher, that is called "using without having announced."
Thus, theft is of six kinds.
The teachers say that the complete avoidance of these six kinds of theft is non-stealing (*asteya*).
For it is also said:
"That which people call 'wealth' is indeed these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) moving outside [the body].
He who takes away another's wealth takes away that person's vital breaths.
For it has been said: "He who steals all one's possessions and he who brings about the end of one's life..."
These two have equal karma; therefore, one should avoid theft.
For the evil-minded thief, there is no world beyond nor this world;
suspected by all beings, he is a malevolent soul and truly wicked.
One who seeks purity and has business here may take earth, water, a vehicle, a leaf, flowers, and even fruits that have not been formally offered.
Rivers, ponds, wells, tanks, and lakes [are likewise available].
One should take [the organs] that are unrestrained by means of the Prājāpatya rite.
Thus, non-stealing is established in this system (tantra). Non-anger is also established in this system.
Why?
Because of the prohibition against Śūdras and because of the instruction regarding excessive austerity.

For here, since endurance toward all pairs of opposites—whether internal, external, or celestial—that have fallen upon the mind and the body, as well as the absence of remedial action, constitute non-anger in this context.
Established in the Tantra:
Furthermore, anger is of four kinds;
namely, that characterized by state, that characterized by action, that which causes deficiency, and that which causes agitation.
Among these, that which is characterized by mental states (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is that in which mental states such as envy, hatred, intoxication, pride, and avarice arise.

That which is characterized by action (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) is that in which actions such as quarreling, enmity, and the wielding of weapons arise. That which causes impairment (*vaikalya-kara*) is that in which actions such as striking with the hands, feet, nose, eyes, or fingers arise.
That which is called "causing agitation" (*udvegakara*) is that wherein one deprives either oneself or another of life.
Thus, anger is of four kinds.
The teachers say that the complete avoidance of these four kinds of anger is "non-anger" (*akrodha*).

Therefore, one who is subject to [the rules] must not give way to anger when there is censure of one's country, caste, family, or occupation; when there is censure of an action performed; when there is censure of a duty; or when there is censure of one's food.
Among these, first, regarding the censure of one's country:
for example, if someone should make a disparaging remark such as, "In the country where you were born, there are no Brahmins at all," one must not give way to anger in that situation.
In this regard, it might be argued that when such a thing is stated, intense mental suffering is manifested.
[Question: How, then, will there be no anger in this case? [Answer: It is said: there will be none.
Why?
Because of the force of the exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*).
Here, in this world of humans, that which is called "place" is a functional aggregate known as the body, which has parents as its cause and is accumulative in nature.
That [state] is existence (*bhava*).
But the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is conscious, all-pervading, and pure.
The difference between him and us is not understood.
Regarding a matter whose meaning is not clearly perceived, you might say this:
"Therefore, since there is no possible cause for anger, anger should not be indulged in by virtue of the power of the enumeration.
This should be understood to apply to the remaining cases as well.
For it also happens that a man is born horned, clawed, fanged, deformed, blood-drinking,
a rākṣasa or a piśāca, and prone to anger.
And it says further: "Men who are devoted to anger are born among vultures, eagles, jackals, gadflies, mosquitoes, and serpents.
Despised by all beings, they have many enemies and few friends."
A man is born cruel in nature, of evil conduct, and prone to anger.
When angry, one commits sins; when angry, one speaks wicked words;
when angry, one becomes shameless; therefore, one should abandon anger.
And so it has been said:

"Whatever one who is angry mutters, whatever he offers in sacrifice, whatever austerity he performs, or whatever he gives—all that merit of his Vaivasvata seizes away; all his learning becomes in vain, and even his tranquility perishes. (PSBh 1.9:207)
Blessed are those tigers among men, those great-souled ones who, by means of their intelligence, extinguish rising anger as one would quench a blazing fire with water.
Where there is beauty, there is knowledge; where there is knowledge, there is austerity.
Where there is austerity, there is success; where there is success, there is forbearance.
Forbearance is the supreme friend of all, while anger is the supreme enemy of all.
This world belongs to those who possess forbearance; the next world belongs to those who possess forbearance.
For this reason, patience must be practiced; thus, non-anger is established in the Tantra.
Likewise, service to the teacher is established in the Tantra.
Why? Because... [PSBh_1.9:213]
[This is known] from both the explanatory teaching and the instruction of the learned.
And here it was said: "We shall explain the rule.
In this context, the particle *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*).
*Ma* occurs in the sense of a proposition (*pratijñā*).
It occurs in the sense of "in me" (*mayi vartate*). It occurs in the sense of "it abides in me" (*mayi tiṣṭhati*).
"If you will abide by what is desired, and if you will remain steadfast, then we shall speak to you.

In this context, "the desired" refers to the eightfold celibate life (*brahmacarya*) that establishes the boundary of conduct. That is to say: one who rises [to greet], rises in response, salutes, performs service for the teacher, acts for his welfare, speaks with ever-increasing excellence, and is the first to rise.
Sleeping last, performing all tasks whether commanded or uncommanded, being grateful, offering himself for all [the teacher's needs], skillful, devoted through courtesy,

and following like a shadow at all times with specific services such as bathing, anointing, and massaging; having the thought, "This has been done," "This will be done," and "What may I do?", he should conduct himself toward the guru day after day.
But he who, having received knowledge from his teacher, bestows it upon many—by this gift of knowledge, his teachers are served.
And when the formal period of studentship has ended, that constant reverence toward the teachers which remains is true studentship (*brahmacarya*).
For it is said: [PSBh_1.9:224] "For it is also so."
The Guru is God, the Guru is the Master, the Guru is the mother, and the Guru is the father;
for one whose conviction is thus established, spiritual welfare is not far off.
By means of fire, the sun, the moon, and the stars, the object of sight is illuminated.
The past, the present, and the future are revealed by the words of the Guru.
Just as travelers traverse a path, just as travelers cross the ocean,
and just as travelers reach heaven— so too is the Guru the guide to liberation.
He who indeed despises the guru, the bestower of immortality,
dwells in hell for sixty thousand years.
Wherever there is censure of the guru, wherever blame of him proceeds, [there one must avoid staying].
In that case, one should cover one's ears or depart elsewhere.
He who always honors the teacher in every circumstance—by him Śiva himself is indeed honored; there is no doubt about this.
Assuming the form of the teacher, Śiva bestows knowledge;
therefore, one who desires the highest good must never disregard the teacher.
[To him] who knows the meaning of the scriptures and constantly shows the way of yoga...
A wise person should always show satisfaction even for a mere trifle.
Whether it be a verse, or half a verse, or a quarter-verse, or even a single syllable—
whichever one receives from another, one must certainly maintain respect toward that person.
"The mother is like the *liṅga*, the father is like the author of the scripture,
and the teacher who provides awakening is the great sanctuary for them.
Thus, service to the teacher is established as a requirement in this Tantra.
In the same way, purity is established in the Tantra.
Why?
Because of the instruction on the ash-bath.
And that purity is threefold:
namely, purity of the body (*gātra-śauca*), purity of disposition (*bhāva-śauca*), and purity of the self (*ātma-śauca*).
Among these, the purity of the body by means of ashes is well known from the instruction regarding the ash-bath (*bhasma-snāna*).
He said: "As for what was stated—that cleansing the body with ashes is well-known—this very point is incorrect.
Why?
Because of the contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
It was stated previously that the well-known restraints (*yama*) consist of non-violence and so forth.
Since it is now further stated here that purification of the body with ashes is [a restraint],
this former and latter statement do not cohere.
And it becomes contradicted;
this is the fault because of the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Therefore, that which was stated—that the cleansing of the body with ashes is well-known—is incorrect.
It is said: this is not a fault.
Why?
Because it is observed in common usage.
In this regard, it is well known elsewhere as well that the body is purified by means of ashes.

For thus it is said: "The defects born of association, those others born of father and mother, and the impurities caused by food and drink that have taken refuge in the body [are all removed by ashes]."

It burns them all to ashes, even those that have reached the marrow of the bones. Furthermore, it is said: "The wise declare that foods defiled by hair or insects, as well as any other impure foods, become fit for consumption as soon as they are touched with ash."
It is further stated:
"Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of one's guru, having committed theft, and even having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one who is smeared with ashes, lying upon a heap of ashes, and reciting the Rudrādhyāya, is liberated from all sins."
He who, with his senses restrained, performs daily the ablution with fire (the *āgneyasnāna*),
shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage and attain the supreme goal.
Thus, it is well known elsewhere as well that purification of the body is accomplished by means of ashes.
Therefore, it is correct to say that non-violence and the other [virtues] are well-known as the *yamas*.

Likewise, by means of ritual ablutions (*upasparśana*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the silent recitation of mantras (*japya*), one becomes pure in mind; thus, purity of intention (*bhāva-śauca*) is established in the *tantra*.
A bath does not remove the corruption that resides within the internal disposition.
Purity of being is the supreme purity; everything else is merely the cleansing of the body.
Even with a thousand loads of earth and a hundred jars of water, those of evil soul whose minds are struck by sin are not purified.
Truthfulness is purity, austerity is purity, restraint of the senses is purity, compassion for all beings is purity; and purification with water is the fifth kind of purity.
For those in whom no longing arises, purity alone is supreme.
Likewise regarding the acceptance [of gifts], the undertaking [of actions], and the range of the sense faculties—for this reason it is said:

"Even if one were to give away all one's possessions with a defiled inner self, one does not partake in merit through that; rather, the state of one's being (*bhāva*) alone is the cause in this matter. (PSBh 1.9:265–266)

"For in whatever way a person forms a virtuous resolve, in that very way all his goals are accomplished; there is no doubt about this. Thus, purity of intention is established as the essential principle in the Tantra.
* Thus, purification of the self is established in the Tantra.
// PSBh_1.9:270 * Because one becomes free from evil through insults, humiliations, censures, and the like; thus, purification of the self is established in the Tantra. // PSBh_1.9:271
For it has been said by others as well:
"For one who wanders over the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves, Manu declared that there is no means of accomplishment superior to insult. (PSBh 1.9:272)
Thus, purity is established in this system.
Likewise, lightness of diet is established in this system.
Why? Because of the instruction regarding alms-food, discarded food, and whatever is obtained as it comes.
Even a very small amount acquired through improper means should be regarded as heavy, whereas even a great deal acquired through proper means should be regarded as light.
For it has been said: "One should practice the 'bee-like' mode of livelihood, which is like a mound of an anthill;
neither angry nor elated—that indeed is eternal austerity."

One who lives by the practice of begging for alms among all kinds of food should eat and accept [gifts] from those who are praiseworthy in their own duties. He should beg for alms from the four castes, but he must avoid those who have fallen from their status.
Milk, water, and alms-food— these are equal, there is no doubt.
However, if a mendicant should discard even a small portion of the remains of his alms-food,
he must perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for every morsel he eats.
The knower of yoga should not practice hoarding, even under any circumstances;
for by the faults arising from hoarding, an ascetic is reborn as a worm.
[He should seek alms] like a bee, without premeditation, before being asked, and without soliciting.
Alms obtained at the appropriate times are traditionally said to be of five kinds.
Wandering from house to house, he should not avoid any particular house;
however, having heard the report of another person, he should avoid a household that is wicked.
If a mendicant should transgress against a virtuous person who is neither corrupt nor fallen,
he gives away that person's merit and takes upon himself their demerit.
And likewise, a mendicant should depart from a householder’s home feeling no expectation.
Taking his merit from sacrifices and charitable works, that mendicant departs.
However, if a mendicant arrives at the house before the Vaiśvadeva offering has been performed,
one should set aside what is intended for the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant.
A mendicant is able to remove the faults incurred by performing the Vaiśvadeva rite,
but the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the faults incurred by a mendicant.
Where alms are not obtained for ten or twelve days, [one should remain there].
A mendicant should avoid that house just as a farmer avoids saline soil.
He should request alms consisting of four syllables;
this is the duty of those who have gone forth, while anything else is merely buying and selling.
Desiring alms, a mendicant should neither laugh nor look about;
he should wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow, but never stand waiting [at a house].
For one who is afraid of old age, death, and rebirth in a womb, and even of hell...
Because one consumes [food] out of fear, it is therefore remembered as *bhaikṣya* (alms-food).
Those who subsist on curds, those who subsist on milk, and others who subsist on barley-gruel—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of one who subsists on *bhaikṣya*.
If one were to drink barley-gruel with cow's urine for twelve years, the color of molten gold, that would not be equal to the merit of begging for alms.
Even if the eldest brother were to drink Soma month after month using only the tip of a blade of Kuśa grass, [it would still not equal the merit of serving the guest].
Alms-food, when not obtained through worldly dealings, may or may not be equivalent [to other food].
Alms-food is the highest good; alms-food is supremely pure.
For alms-food is the best for those observing vows; alms-food alone is the supreme goal.
Whatever water is unfit for drinking when it is in water-closets becomes fit for drinking again once it has entered a river;
likewise, food and drink that have been brought according to the prescribed rule do not become defiled if they have passed through the vessel of a twice-born man.
Whether it be salty or unsalted, oily or dry, flavorful or flavorless, whether the food is solid or liquid— [it remains pure].

If one here consumes blameless alms-food, he indeed becomes a bhikṣu, not fallen from the dharma of a bhikṣu. Furthermore, regarding what has been relinquished (*utsṛṣṭa*) and what is obtained as it comes (*yathālabdha*), since the appropriate occasion for them has arrived, we shall provide an exposition of their meaning according to the aphorisms (*sūtra*), as established by the tenets of our own specific system (*pratitantrasiddhānta*). Thus, lightness of food is established in this treatise (*tantra*).
Likewise, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is established in the Tantra.
Why?
Because of the instruction on heedfulness and because of the instruction on recitation (*japa*).
In this regard, one must always be vigilant regarding the restraints (*yama*) and maintain established mindfulness.
For it has been said: "Vigilance, self-control, and renunciation are declared to be the horses of a Brahmin;
by means of these, which are joined with the reins of virtuous conduct (*śīla*), the self should be placed upon the chariot of the mind."
Having ascended that chariot of Brahman, cutting through the bonds of fear of death— those consisting of conception, birth, and old age— he remains established as Brahman.
Thus, vigilance is established in this Tantra.
Thus, non-violence and the other [virtues] are well-known as the *yamas*.
[Objection: They are not well-known as *yamas* because of the fault of lack of distinction;
for here, non-violence and the others are also means for accomplishing *dharma* for others.
And here too in this treatise, they are exactly those [same ones].
Therefore, there is no distinction even regarding their culmination in the probandum and the probans.
It is said: "No."
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anekānta*).

If, on the grounds of the mere similarity of being a means of establishing a property (*dharma-sādhanāstitva-mātra-sādharmya*), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth were to be abandoned, then for that same reason, the categories of cause and effect, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), pleasure and pain, saṃsāra, and other such entities would also have to be abandoned.
Now, [if it is argued that] there is no such non-uniqueness (*anekānta*):
furthermore, if [the injunction were merely to abandon], it would follow that acts such as killing would become means for achieving dharma through their abandonment.

Furthermore, it is established that the injunction consists of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), because it includes excessive giving, excessive sacrifice, excessive austerity, excessive movement, non-returning, and so forth.
And because of the specific qualification of the rule (*niyama*), there is no lack of distinction.
Therefore, it is rightly said that non-violence and the others are the well-known restraints (*yamas*).
For this reason, it was stated: "of Mahādeva, the Right-Faced One" (*dakṣiṇāmūrti*).
* Herein ends this section on Yama.
* It is asked: what is the measure for one dwelling in that abode?
* That must be stated, as in the case of the householder and others.
This is said: No.
Because it says:
Wearing a single garment. (PS 1.10)
* Here, "one" refers to the number.
* "Clothing" (vāsa) occurs in the sense of covering.
* His clothing is of five kinds: born from eggs, born from worms, born from hair, born from bark, or born from skin.

Whatever is obtained through wholesome means— whether it be a single garment or many garments— that is free from worldly attachments, sufficient merely to cover the private parts, and serves to counteract shame, such a single garment is to be accepted. By the very force of this rule, once the renunciation of all possessions has been performed, the disciple is to be consecrated while retaining only a single garment.
He asks: "When does his cessation of shame occur?
It is said: "By means of knowledge and the absence of impurity.
In this context, when he has attained knowledge and his impurities are exhausted, then there is the cessation of his shame.
He asks: "Even when modesty has ceased, must one necessarily wear a single garment, or is it optional?
It is said: it is optional, because [the text] says:
"Or without clothing" (PS 1.11).

Here, the syllable "a" functions in the sense of a prohibition regarding clothing. One should exist like one who is born—naked, without clothing, and without possessions. He asks: "What is the purpose of being without clothing?"
That must be stated, just as in the case of "wearing a single garment.
It is said that two purposes are to be seen: for the sake of signifying the absence of possessions and for the sake of proclaiming it as inauspicious.
The word *vā* (or) is used for the deliberation between capability and incapability.
If one is incapable [of such practice], then one should be unclothed and wear but a single garment;
if one is capable, then one should be without garments, naked, like one just born, and free from possessions—this is the meaning.
"Or" (*vā*) does not indicate an alternative (*vikalpa*).
The meaning is: "because conceptual constructions and objects are impossible.

[The opponent] asks: Must one who dwells in that abode remain there until the fall of the body, never departing, fixed solely in meditation like a stone; or is departure from that abode observed, such as entering villages and the like for the sake of obtaining ashes, alms, water, and so forth?
It is said that [the rule] has been observed, because:
"One should not look at urine or excrement. (PS 1.12)

In this context, "urine and feces" (*mūtrapurīṣam*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*) used in the sense of conjunction (*ca*). Here, "urine" (*mūtra*) refers to that which remains in the belly, which subsequently issues forth and flows out; that is urine. It is called "urine" (*mūtra*) because of its being emitted (*mocanāt*).
The meaning is that urine is well-known in the world and other contexts because of its connection with the state of being urine (*mūtratva*).

That which is called feces (*purīṣa*) is the specific food—whether drunk, chewed, or licked—that has been digested by the internal fire and is discharged by the downward wind (*apāna*); that is feces.

The meaning is that it is well-known in the world and other contexts as "feces" (*purīṣa*) either because it has gone out from before (*pura*), or because of its connection with the state of being feces (*purīṣatva*).
The syllable *na* serves to negate perception;
its meaning is "it is not to be perceived.
The prefix *ava-* signifies relinquishing, which means negation both in the sense of abandoning a genus and in the sense of negating other sense organs.
*Īkṣ* means "seeing. Regarding this innate faculty of perception, the eye: by means of this eye and this intellect, one should not look upon the urine and feces of humans and the like;
however, the meaning is that one should not [look upon such things] in the case of cows and the like.
[The opponent] asks: Is it only the appearance of urine and excrement that is prohibited for this [mirror]?
[The author] replies: No.
One should not address a woman or a Śūdra with the Veda.

* Here, "woman and Śūdra" (*strīśūdra*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the sense of "and. * In this context, "woman" refers to that being well-known in the world, possessing breasts, hips, and hair, endowed with gestures, expressions, and charms, characterized by the nature of the male state, whether divine or human, consisting of supreme passion, and having the form of a sensual object.
Having considered this, [the rule] is prohibited.
Since its application will occur preceded by a restatement, the meaning is that one should not speak to a woman.
This so-called Śūdra is well-known in the world and elsewhere as the attendant of the three [higher] castes.
A Śūdra [is so called] because of grieving and because of being malicious. He is indeed prohibited on the grounds that he is merciless.
For what purpose?
* Thus, when reviled or struck, one becomes angry and proceeds toward killing him; consequently, there occurs a loss of birth, knowledge, austerity, and learning.

// PSBh_1.13:9 * Furthermore, since the absence of contempt and so forth has been indicated, from that absence of contempt and so forth, there follows the absence of the indicator and the one who grows [in status].
// PSBh_1.13:10 * And we shall provide the exposition of this fault in the *akaluṣa-sūtra*. // PSBh_1.13:11
The syllable *na* signifies a prohibition of speaking;
the meaning is "one must not speak. The word *abhi* signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*).
The meaning is: "in the case of a negation, both when there is the apprehension of a genus (*jāti*) and when there is the negation of the other.
[The root] *bhāṣ* [is used] in the sense of "distinct speech" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*). "Speech" (*vāk*) refers to that which is the organ of action (*karmendriya*), by means of which one speaks.

Therefore, the meaning is that one should not speak to a woman or a Śūdra. [Objection: It has been stated that "one should neither look at nor speak to them"; what then, must this practitioner remain like a blind man or a mute? [Reply: No, it is not so.
For it says:
"If he should look [at her], if he should speak to her... (PS 1.14).
* Here, the phrase "if... if" (*yadi yadi*) expresses a hypothetical contingency (*āśaṅkā*).

[One might object: Since there is the injunction "one shall not speak," even though the act is prohibited, for one who has entered a village or similar place for the sake of the teacher or for his own sake—such as for the purpose of obtaining ashes, alms, or water—the sight and conversation with women and Śūdras regarding feces and urine will nonetheless occur.
Having done so, therefore this was said by the omniscient Blessed One: "If he were to look, if he were to speak.
The meaning is that [the result] would necessarily come to be.
He asks: "When one has been looked upon or addressed by someone who is afflicted, what expiation (*nirghātana*) should be performed?
It is said: "Sprinkling with water (*upasparśana*).
Because: [the following verse follows].
Having sipped water.

* Here, "upa" signifies acceptance (*abhyupagama*). // PSBh_1.15:1 * The meaning is: by means of acceptance, [it is done] by one of defiled intellect. // PSBh_1.15:2 * "To touch" (*spṛśya*) means precisely the joining of the body with the substance of ashes. // PSBh_1.15:3
